segments.title: Why journalists can use anonymous sources but historians cannot
segments.summary: Journalists can vet protected sources while reporting urgent events, whereas historians must leave an evidence trail that another scholar can inspect and test.
segments.body: Journalists often cover events while they are unfolding, when the public needs information and an informed source may speak only if protected from professional or personal consequences. Anonymity can make it easier for that person to speak honestly. The reporter can meet the source, discuss and substantiate the evidence in real time, and decide whether to trust the account even when the public cannot see the source's identity. A joke about ancient Greek predecessors receiving information in dreams introduces the modern historian's obligation to provide evidence that others can check. Another historian should theoretically be able to follow the same list of sources and substantiate at least the evidentiary part of an argument and analysis. An anonymous source whose identity and context cannot be recovered breaks that chain.
segments.question: Why can journalists use anonymous sources when historians generally cannot?
segments.answerShort: A journalist can personally assess a protected source while reporting a current event, but a historian must provide an evidence trail that later researchers can independently check.

evidence.note: Immediate reporting may depend on sources whose anonymity protects them from consequences and makes honesty easier, while the journalist can assess them directly.
The ancient Greek dream joke precedes the requirement that another historian can theoretically follow the same sources and substantiate at least the evidentiary part of an argument and analysis.

segments.title: Anonymous newspaper sources turn historians into detectives
segments.summary: Anonymous attribution in contemporary newspapers can force historians to reconstruct who supplied a claim before treating the report as dependable evidence.
segments.body: A newspaper article from the period does not automatically solve the historian's source problem if its decisive information came from an unnamed person. Without knowing who spoke, the researcher cannot readily substantiate the report or judge whether to trust its information. Research into 1920s and 1930s newspapers can therefore involve reconstructing who could have leaked a claim and which journalist or paper received it. The 1900s papers supply a related, sometimes amusing example: attempts to conceal a source can leave the person's identity obvious. This detective work complicates research, but it supports analysis whose evidentiary basis other historians can check.

evidence.note: He explains why anonymously sourced contemporary journalism remains difficult for historians to trust.
Substantiation supports historical analysis but can require detective work to identify who leaked information to whom in 1920s and 1930s newspapers.
The 1900s newspapers are singled out for amusing attempts to conceal an otherwise obvious source of information.
The conclusion ties this evidentiary problem to historians' different treatment of sources.
